verses.translation_literal: A song, a psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song, a psalm, set down for David.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is verse 1 in the Hebrew, though the KJV leaves it unnumbered, so every verse number after it differs by one. The title strings two words for music together: shir, a song for voices, and mizmor, a piece for strings or an instrument. Perform it as both. The line 'of David' (ledavid) can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the David tradition'; the title does not say which.

This psalm is not new material. Radak, Meiri and Malbim all observe that it is two older psalms joined: the first half is the end of Psalm 57 (David hiding from Saul in a cave) and the second half is the end of Psalm 60 (a war song after defeat). Malbim says the editor joined them to sing of the rescue of one man and the rescue of a nation together. Radak reads the whole as spoken by the exiles, and by one of David's line who will reign. Play the psalm as a man who has already been saved once and is asking again.

philological_notes.note: A psalm: a song sung to an instrument. It comes from the same root as 'I will sing praises' in verse 2 (אזמרה), so the title and the first act of the psalm are one word.

verses.translation_literal: Steadfast [is] my heart, O God; I will sing, and I will sing praises, even my glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: My heart is set, O God. It does not shake. I will sing, and I will make music on the strings, and my very soul will sing with me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open on stillness, not noise. The first word, nakhon, is 'firmly set', the way a foundation is set or a stand is fixed. The KJV's 'fixed' is close; the BBE and YLT ('prepared') lose the sense of something that holds. Radak hears a speaker who has waited years for rescue and has not given up, so the heart is steady in trust, not only ready to perform.

The two verbs are a pair on one root family: ashirah is singing with the mouth, azamerah is playing music (Radak: 'with the mouth' and 'with an instrument'). The KJV, 'sing and give praise', turns the second into something less musical. Then comes the odd last word, 'my glory'. 'Glory' (kavod) is used here for the self, the soul, the best part of a person (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion). The KJV's 'even with my glory' makes it an accessory to the singing; the Hebrew has no 'with', and the glory is a second singer. Rashi offers another reading: out of respect for his own honor he will not hold back.

philological_notes.note: Firm, established, set in place. Rashi glosses it as 'faithful with you'; Radak takes it as a heart that stays confident of God's goodness despite exile.
Literally 'my glory'. Used for the soul or inner self, the 'glory' of the body, so it is a poetic parallel to 'my heart'.

token_glosses.gloss: and I will sing praises with an instrument

verses.translation_literal: Awake, the lyre and harp! I will awaken dawn.
verses.translation_dramatic: Wake, lyre. Wake, harp. The sky is still grey, and I will be the one to wake the dawn.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker gives orders to his instruments as if they were servants asleep in the dark. The verb is the same twice: ura, 'awake!' to the strings, and a'irah, 'I will wake' the dawn. Hebrew makes the man the one who rouses the day; the usual order of things is reversed. Rashi says it plainly: other kings are woken by the dawn, and I wake the dawn. Do not play it as a boast. He is up in the night because he cannot sleep for praise, and the strings answer.

The KJV, 'I myself will awake early', loses the pun entirely, and the object disappears: it is the dawn, shachar, he wakes, not himself. The BBE is further off. Radak lets both readings stand: he is waking the instruments, or waking himself. The rabbis (Rashi, Meiri, citing Berakhot 3b) tell of a harp hung over David's bed that the north wind played at midnight. Treat that as a later story about this verse, not part of the text.

The nevel and kinnor are both stringed instruments. The nevel is a larger harp or lyre and the kinnor a smaller lyre; English 'psaltery and harp' is a guess of the 1611 translators. Shachar is also the name of a Canaanite dawn god known from Ugarit; whether the psalmist hears that here is my own reading, and it would make him the one who rouses the god's own hour.

philological_notes.note: 'I will wake', the causative of the same root as ura, 'awake!'. The repetition is the point: the instruments wake, and he wakes the dawn. Ibn Ezra, noting a view of 'Rabbi Moshe', takes it as a transitive verb.
Dawn, first light. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'morning'.

verses.translation_literal: I will thank you among the peoples, YHWH, and I will sing praises to you among the nations.
verses.translation_dramatic: Among the peoples I will give you thanks, LORD. Among the nations I will make music to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene widens: from a dark room and a few strings to an open place with strangers in it. The psalmist does not sing only to Israel. 'Among the peoples' and 'among the nations' are a matched pair (amim and leummim), and the second halves of both lines are the second halves of the first verse, thanks and then song. The KJV, 'among the people', takes the Hebrew plural as a singular and loses the other nations; the second line 'nations' catches it, but the first does not.

The word for 'thank' (odekha) is the same verb as 'confess' or 'praise': to say aloud what someone has done. It is public speech, not private feeling. Ibn Ezra hears a difference of time: quiet song at dawn, open song by day. Radak reads 'peoples' as the whole world coming to Jerusalem at the redemption.

philological_notes.note: 'I will thank you', hiphil of ידה: to acknowledge, confess, thank aloud. A public act, hence 'among the peoples'.
'Among the nations'. Radak notes the lamed is written without a dagesh although the root has one; it is a soft form of the same word.

token_glosses.gloss: and I will sing praises to you

verses.translation_literal: For great, above the heavens, [is] your covenant loyalty, and to the clouds, your faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your steadfast love is taller than the heavens. Your faithfulness climbs to the clouds and does not stop.
verses.directors_commentary:
The singer measures God's character by height, the one dimension no one can check. Notice the two prepositions: covenant loyalty (chesed) goes 'above' the heavens, faithfulness (emet) only 'to' the clouds. The rabbis felt the difference and tied it to Psalm 57:11, where the same pair appears with 'to the heavens'. Rashi, citing Pesachim 50b, says one verse speaks of those who act for the right reason (lishmah), which reaches above the heavens, and the other of those who do not, which reaches only to the heavens. Radak reads it as the exile and return: chesed is the surplus, the nations themselves carrying Israel home, while emet is only what was promised and is owed. Meiri, by contrast, takes the whole as hyperbole of praise. Play it as a swelling, not a calculation.

The KJV's 'mercy' flattens chesed, which is loyalty owed inside a bond; the covenant is the point. 'Truth' for emet is also thin: the word means what holds firm, reliability. And the KJV's 'reacheth unto the clouds' adds a verb the Hebrew does not have, so the second line there lunges where the Hebrew simply arrives. The shachaqim are the thin dust-like upper skies, the farthest thing an eye can see (Ibn Ezra).

philological_notes.note: Loyalty that goes beyond what the bond requires; 'mercy' (KJV) loses the covenant frame. Here its height exceeds even the heavens.
'From above', hence 'beyond'. Contrast the 'ad ('to, as far as') of the second line and of Psalm 57:11; the rabbis read the difference as a difference of motive.
The upper sky or clouds, literally the 'fine, thin' things; Ibn Ezra says nothing visible is higher.

verses.translation_literal: Be exalted over [the] heavens, God, and over all the earth, your glory.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, God, above the heavens. And over every inch of earth, your glory.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a command, and a bold one: rumah, 'be high', said to God. Radak and Meiri hear a figure of speech: in exile it is as though God is not high, not ruling, so the singer asks him to be seen as he is. Ibn Ezra reads it as a consequence of the previous verse: show your height by saving me. Metzudat David adds that even a weak ruler is called mighty if he sits on high, so the prayer asks God to act like what he is.

The second line has no verb at all. The Hebrew just says 'and over all the earth, your glory', and the 'be' carries across from line one. The KJV, like the Hebrew, leaves it verbless ('and thy glory above all the earth'); 'above' there is the Hebrew 'al, the same preposition as in line one, so the repetition of 'al (over, over) is the sound of the verse. The KJV's 'O God' is also moved: in Hebrew the vocative comes after 'heavens', delaying the name and letting the heavens fill the first beat. Note the echo of Psalm 57:12 and the verse's role as the refrain that opens the hope of the whole battle poem: height first, then earth.

philological_notes.note: Imperative 'be high/be exalted' (with the -ah ending that makes it urgent). A jussive wish, not a statement.
Repeated in both lines ('over the heavens... over all the earth'); the repetition builds the sweep from sky to ground.
'Your glory', literally 'your weight'. Left without a verb, it reads as an acclamation more than a request.

verses.translation_literal: So that your beloved ones may be rescued: save [with] your right [hand], and answer me.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that those you love may be pulled free. Save us with your right hand, and answer me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns from song to request, and it is the hinge of the whole piece. The plea 'save' is hedged by a purpose clause: le-ma'an, 'for the sake that'. The speaker asks, but for the sake of others. 'Your beloved ones' (yedidekha) is plural, and the root ידד is close in sound to David's own name, which the ear catches in a psalm of David. The KJV's 'thy beloved' reads as singular in English. The verb yechaltzun is 'be pulled out, drawn out', used for sandals pulled off and soldiers armed or delivered; it has a physical pull. The KJV's 'delivered' is gentler.

The right hand is where strength is and where the sword is held. 'Answer me' is the sudden change from the plural 'beloved ones' to a single voice. The ASV and YLT render 'answer us'; the Hebrew form here has 'me', and it is the speaker's own voice again. Rashi says why: all the people hang on him. Metzudat David reads 'answer me too'.

philological_notes.note: 'May they be rescued', literally drawn or pulled out. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'taking out'.
'Those you love', plural. The same root family as David's name (דוד), which may be why the verse sits so near it.

verses.translation_literal: God has spoken in his holiness: I will exult, I will divide up Shechem, and the valley of Succoth I will measure off.
verses.translation_dramatic: God has spoken from his holy place. And I will exult. I will cut Shechem into shares. I will take a measuring line to the valley of Succoth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. Until now the speaker has been asking; now he reports an answer. 'God has spoken' is in the perfect tense: it is already said. The oracle is the ground for everything else, and nothing in it is plea.

The Hebrew says 'in his holiness' (bekodsho), which can be 'in his sanctuary' or 'by his holiness' (as an oath). The KJV, 'in his holiness', keeps the ambiguity. The Targum picks the place: from the house of his presence. The speaker's name for God is Elohim throughout this psalm, not YHWH after verse 4.

The verbs are the language of a land survey: achalleqah is 'I will divide into shares', amadded is 'I will measure with a line'. These are the actions of one who hands out an inheritance. Shechem, the old city of the north, and the valley of Succoth, east of the Jordan, are named as places to be divided. There is a pun in Shechem: the name also means 'shoulder' and so 'portion', as in Jacob's gift to Joseph in Genesis 48:22, which Rashi cites. The KJV's 'I will rejoice' softens e'lozah, which is a loud, physical exulting.

philological_notes.note: 'I will exult', a strong, bodily joy. 'Rejoice' in the KJV is weaker.
The city, and also 'shoulder' or 'portion'. Rashi ties this verse to Genesis 48:22 ('one shekhem above your brothers'), and Metzudat Zion to the 'shoulder' sense.

verses.translation_literal: Mine [is] Gilead, mine [is] Manasseh, and Ephraim [is] the protection of my head; Judah [is] my lawgiver.
verses.translation_dramatic: Gilead is mine. Manasseh is mine. Ephraim is the helmet on my head, and Judah is the staff in my hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
God is still speaking, and the speech is a list of what belongs to the speaker. Each name is a tribe or a region of the Israelite heartland: Gilead and Manasseh east of the Jordan, Ephraim in the hill country, Judah in the south. The repetition 'mine, mine' is a claim of possession, and the order runs from east to west and then to the royal tribe.

The word ma'oz is 'stronghold' or 'protection', and the phrase 'protection of my head' makes Ephraim a helmet. The KJV's 'strength of mine head' is archaic and vague. The last word, mechokeki, is where the English versions part. The KJV 'lawgiver' follows the root חקק, to cut or decree, and the ASV's 'sceptre' reads it as a ruler's staff, which is how STEPBible has it. Metzudat Zion says the officers are called mechokekim because they set the laws. Whatever the rendering, Judah is the tribe the ruler comes from. Metzudat David sees the whole verse as David looking past the split of the kingdom to a time when all are under him. That is the traditional commentary's reading, not something the verse says.

philological_notes.note: A place of refuge or defense. 'The ma'oz of my head' is protective gear, a helmet, not just 'strength'.
'My lawgiver' or 'my ruler's staff'. Metzudat Zion says officers are called mechokekim because they set the laws.

verses.translation_literal: Moab [is] the basin of my washing; over Edom I throw my sandal; over Philistia I shout in triumph.
verses.translation_dramatic: Moab is the basin I wash in. On Edom I throw my sandal. Over Philistia I raise the shout of victory.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the neighboring peoples, each with a gesture of contempt. Moab is a sir rachtzi: the 'pot of my washing', a basin for washing feet or hands. Nations are reduced to household crockery. The KJV's 'washpot' is accurate and, to its credit, does not clean it up; keep the humiliation. Rashi, true to the setting, says it means my servant, used like a utensil.

The sandal thrown 'over' Edom is a gesture the text leaves unexplained. Rashi reads it as Edom's kings taking my sandals off my feet, which is service. A thrown sandal can also be a sign of taking possession of land; the text does not say which, and the reading of ownership is my own, not a cited one. The KJV's 'cast out my shoe' is accurate to the Hebrew and keeps the puzzle.

The last line breaks the pattern. Moab and Edom are humbled; Philistia is shouted at. The verb etro'a'a is the war cry (teru'ah) of Israel's army, a loud, deliberate noise to frighten the enemy (Rashi, Metzudat David). The KJV's 'will I triumph' is abstract. Perform it as a shout.

philological_notes.note: 'Pot of my washing': a basin. A deliberate image of lowest use. Rashi reads it as 'my servant, a utensil I use'.
'I shout in triumph', the war-shout of victory, related to teru'ah.

verses.translation_literal: Who will bring me [to] a city of fortification? Who has led me to Edom?
verses.translation_dramatic: But who will bring me to the fortified city? Who has led me, even as far as Edom?
verses.directors_commentary:
The boast of the last three verses meets a wall. Two questions, one after the other, begin with the same word, mi, 'who?', and the confidence of the oracle drains. Edom is the hard target: a mountain country of cliffs and fortified rock cities to the southeast, and a stronghold (mivtzar) is exactly what such a land had. The speaker has been told it will be his, but he does not see how he gets there.

The two verbs differ in tense: yovileni is 'will bring me' (a future), while nachani is 'has led me' (a perfect), so the second question looks back as well as forward. The KJV and BBE make both futures. Both verbs are about being taken by someone else. Metzudat David reads it as: who gives me the strength to take a fortified town? Rashi, as often, connects it with David's defeat of Edom in the Valley of Salt (2 Samuel 8:13). The psalm does not say the city is Petra or any named place. The questions have no answer in this verse. The answer comes only in the next.

philological_notes.note: 'He has led me' (perfect); Metzudat Zion glosses it as guiding or driving. The tense is a quiet shift from the future of 'who will bring me'.

verses.translation_literal: Have you not, O God, rejected us? And you do not go out, O God, with our armies.
verses.translation_dramatic: Is it not you, God, who cast us off? You, God, who no longer march out with our armies.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to the two questions is an accusation, and it is addressed to the one who was just promised a victory. The speaker says there is only one who could lead him, and he has walked away. Nothing in the verse is soft. Zanach is 'to cast off, reject', a word used for throwing something away that no longer pleases; the KJV's 'cast us off' keeps it.

There is a grammar problem. The first word, halo, is the question 'is it not?', but the second half has the plain negative lo with no question mark. The ASV reads both as statements; the KJV, 'Wilt not thou', turns both into questions about the future, which the Hebrew does not say. I keep the first as a question and the second as a plain statement. 'Go out' (teze) is the verb for an army marching to war, and 'armies' (tzeva'ot) is the word in 'the LORD of Hosts'. The people have armies, but their God does not go out with them.

Metzudat David finds comfort in it: the distress came from God, so the rescue will too. The Targum is blunter and adds the reason, because we sinned. That addition is not in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: 'You have rejected us', cast us off. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'abandoned'.
'With our armies'. Metzudat Zion defines it as an army that goes out to war. The plural is the same word as in the title 'LORD of Hosts'.

verses.translation_literal: Give to us help from [the] foe, and worthless [is the] deliverance of man.
verses.translation_dramatic: Help us against the enemy. Whatever rescue a man can give is empty breath.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a flat, practical plea. The verb havah is a short, almost rough 'give here', the same word used for 'come now' in Genesis 11:3, so the imperative is bare, with no polite frame. The second line is a verdict, spoken as if closing a ledger: shav', 'emptiness, nothing', is the word for worthless, vain things, and it is set against teshu'ah, 'deliverance', the word of salvation itself. Metzudat David reads it directly: you give us help against the oppressor, because human rescue has no use.

The pair 'ezrah and teshu'ah (help, deliverance) lines up two kinds of help, God's and man's, and the poem has just asked who will lead it to Edom. The answer is no one human. For mitsar, the KJV and Webster choose 'trouble', which turns the foe into a condition; ASV 'adversary' follows the other reading. Both are possible: the same consonants give 'narrowness' (distress) and 'the one who narrows', the enemy. The KJV's 'vain' is fair, but 'man' is adam, the whole human race, not a single warrior, so the verdict covers every king and every army. Play it quietly, almost tired: they have tried.

philological_notes.note: From a root meaning 'to be narrow'. It can be the noun 'distress' (KJV 'trouble') or the 'foe' who narrows (ASV, STEPBible). The literal layer takes 'foe'.
Emptiness, worthlessness, what lacks substance. The flat predicate that opens the second line before its subject.
Humankind in general, not a single person: the verdict is on every human power.

verses.translation_literal: In God we will do strength, and he, he will tread down our foes.
verses.translation_dramatic: With God we will do mighty things. And it is he, he himself, who will trample down those who hem us in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a note of trust, and the actor should sing it, not shout it. The turn from the plea of verse 13 is sudden: the same people who were asking for help now say what they will do, and in the same breath say that the real doer is someone else. 'We will do strength; he will tread down' is a division of labour: the army marches, but the victory is credited to God.

'Do strength' (עשה חיל) is an idiom, and the KJV's 'do valiantly' reads it fairly, but it hides the plain sound of the phrase: חַיִל is the word for an army, a force, a fortune or a woman of worth, so 'to do חַיִל' is to act with force and substance. The verb יָבוּס, 'he will tread down', is an image of the warrior setting his foot on the conquered, a gesture ancient Near Eastern kings carved on their monuments, and the KJV's 'tread down' keeps it. It is a verb of the threshing floor and the vineyard as much as of battle: the enemy becomes trampled straw. The doubled 'and he, he' (וְהוּא with the verb) in the Hebrew points to God alone; the KJV's 'for he it is that shall' catches it, though it adds the word 'for'.

The verse also closes the psalm on the word צָרֵינוּ, 'our foes', the same root as 'foe' in verse 13, which gives the unit a ring: the one who is asked to help against the צַר is the one who will tread the צָרִים down.

philological_notes.note: 'We will do strength': an idiom for acting with force or valour. חַיִל is also 'army' and 'wealth'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'strength and courage'.
'He will tread down', a verb of trampling and treading underfoot. Metzudat Zion links it to the same root in Isaiah 14:19, where a corpse is 'trodden down'.
